Press enter or click to view image in full size React Native JavaScript Open Source Cpp Jsdom 4 min read 5 hours ago -- Sometimes you get handed a piece of HTML with a small script embedded in it, and all you actually need is to run that script and read one value back out. A countdown timer that computes how many days are left, a greeting that gets built from a user’s name, a discount badge that does a bit of math before it shows a number. You don’t need to show any of that HTML on screen. You just need the DOM to exist long enough for the script to run against it. On a website this is trivial, you drop the thing in an iframe and let the browser handle it. React Native has no iframe. So the usual move is a WebView, mounted somewhere off-screen, just so that one script has a DOM to run against. It works, but it’s a strange amount of machinery for the job. You’re loading a full browser engine and mounting it in your component tree just to run a script and read a value back. It’s slow to spin up, awkward to test, and it turns something that should be plain logic into a UI problem. Node ran into the same wall years ago and solved it with jsdom: spin up a DOM in memory, run your script against it, read the result back, throw the whole thing away. No browser, no window, nothing on screen. React Native never had its own version of that. So we built one. react-native-nitro-jsdom It’s a headless HTML/DOM sandbox for React Native. You give it HTML, it parses a real DOM, and you can run real JavaScript against it, all off-screen and outside the React tree. import { JSDOM } from 'react-native-nitro-jsdom'const dom = JSDOM.create(`

`) await dom.evaluate(` document.getElementById('result').textContent = String(2 + 2) `) const value = await dom.evaluate(`document.getElementById('result').textContent`) // → "4" const html = dom.serialize() dom.dispose() No component involved, nothing rendered, no JSON getting serialized back and forth across a bridge. You create a sandbox, use it, dispose of it, same as any other bit of native state you manage yourself. How it works Three pieces, each doing one job: Nitro Modules handles the native binding layer. Calls go straight through JSI, synchronously, no bridge in the middle. Lexbor, a WHATWG-compliant HTML parser written in C99, owns the actual DOM tree: querySelector, attributes, serialization. QuickJS, a JS engine built for embedding, runs the scripts, each one in its own isolated runtime. TypeScript (consumer) │ │ synchronous JSI call ▼ Nitro Module (C++ binding layer) │ ├──► Lexbor → HTML parsing, DOM tree, querySelector, serialize() └──► QuickJS → isolated JS runtime, window/document stubs, executes scriptsPeople usually ask why we didn’t just reuse Hermes, since React Native already ships it. Hermes is one shared runtime for your whole app, it isn’t built to be spun up and torn down per sandbox. QuickJS is built for exactly that: cheap, throwaway, fully isolated runtimes. Every JSDOM.create() gets its own engine, its own globals, its own event loop, walled off from everything else running in your app. evaluate() is the only way in. Every read and every mutation is a JavaScript string that runs inside QuickJS and talks to Lexbor underneath. Having one entry point like that is what makes it safe to embed, there’s no path for sandboxed code to reach back out into the rest of your app. Where this is useful beyond the one example The countdown timer is the concrete case, but the same idea, treat HTML as data with logic attached, without touching your real UI, applies wherever you’d otherwise reach for something heavier: • Sanitizing or transforming untrusted HTML before it ever touches your component tree • Running personalization scripts a server team ships without waiting on your app’s next release • Testing HTML-generating logic without needing a device or a simulator behind it Roughly, the trade-off looks like this: With a hidden WebView ❌ • Needs a React component to mount • Can’t run off the React tree • Isolation between instances is complex to manage • Memory control is limited, garbage collection handles it • Overhead of a full browser engine just to run a script With react-native-nitro-jsdom ✅ • No component needed • Runs fully headless, off the React tree • Every instance is natively isolated • Full memory control via dispose() • Overhead of two small engines, built for exactly this Try it yarn add react-native-nitro-jsdom react-native-nitro-modulesIt’s built entirely on Nitro Modules, so you need the New Architecture enabled and React Native 0.76 or newer. iOS, Android, and visionOS all work today. It’s still early, and there’s a lot of DOM surface left to cover. If you run into a gap, or you just want to poke around the code and see how a piece of it works, contributions and issues are welcome, everything is open on GitHub. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs cover the rest, API reference, architecture notes, and the roadmap.
